findings.name: Conv2d
findings.title: Discrete cross-correlation
findings.equation: y[c,i,j] = b[c] + Σ_k Σ_u Σ_v W[c,k,u,v] · x[k, s·i + d·u − p, s·j + d·v − p]
freedom: The same 288 weights are reused at every one of the 784 positions. That reuse is the whole idea: it assumes what matters is the same everywhere in the image, and it is why a convolution has so few parameters for what it does.
Dilation widens the window without adding a single parameter: d=1 already reaches 3 pixels using 3×3 weights. Stacking dilations 1,2,4,8 grows the reach exponentially with depth.

Groups divide the parameters by g. At g=C_in each filter sees one channel — that is a depthwise convolution, 9 parameters instead of 288, and a 1×1 convolution after it mixes the channels back. That factorisation is most of what makes mobile architectures small.

findings.name: BatchNorm2d
findings.title: Batch normalization
arithmetic: unchanged — this rescales, it does not reshape
64 running statistics, updated but not trained by the optimizer
freedom: The statistics come from the batch, so what this layer computes for one sample depends on the others beside it. That is why small batches hurt it and why it behaves differently in eval mode, where the running statistics take over.
γ and β let the network undo the normalization if that is better — initialising γ=0 in a residual branch starts the block as the identity, which is a common trick for training very deep stacks.
LayerNorm takes the statistics per sample instead, so batch size stops mattering. That is why transformers use it.

findings.name: Activation
findings.title: relu — pointwise nonlinearity
freedom: Zero below the origin, identity above. The gradient is 0 or 1, which is why it trains well and why a unit stuck below zero never recovers.
Without something like this the whole network collapses: any stack of affine maps is one affine map. This is the only reason depth adds expressive power.
It acts on each number alone, so it can bend the function but never mix information between positions.

findings.name: MaxPool2d
findings.title: Max pooling
findings.equation: y[c,i,j] = max over the window  x[c, s·i+u, s·j+v]
arithmetic: none — the operation has nothing to learn
freedom: Max is a hard selection: the gradient reaches only the winning element, so the rest of the window learns nothing from this step. Mean spreads it evenly.
Max keeps the strongest response and discards where in the window it was. That invariance is useful for recognition and harmful for anything needing precise location.
A strided convolution downsamples too, and learns how rather than being told. It costs parameters; pooling costs none.

findings.name: Flatten
findings.title: Reinterpretation
findings.equation: y[n] = x[i,j,k]   with n = (i·H + j)·W + k
freedom: Nothing is computed here. The same values are read as one long vector.
What it costs comes next: a dense layer on 6,272 inputs needs 6,272 weights per output. Pooling first is how that bill is avoided.
Because the ordering is positional, the layer after it treats position 37 as a fixed meaning — which is why flattening destroys translation invariance that the convolutions built.

findings.name: Linear
findings.title: Affine map
arithmetic: 10, because you set it — a dense layer's width is a choice, not a consequence
freedom: Every output sees every input, so cost grows as the product of the two widths. That product is usually where a network's parameters go.
Two of these in a row with nothing between them multiply to a single matrix W₂W₁ — the depth buys nothing without a nonlinearity.

Factorising W ≈ UV with U ∈ ℝ^(out×r), V ∈ ℝ^(r×in) costs r×(6,272+10) instead of 62,720. Below r ≈ 9 it is cheaper, and it constrains the map to rank r — sometimes a useful prior rather than only a saving.
